findings.text: Command A sits on the Pareto frontier between correctly answering and refusing for both enterprise safety modes (contextual and strict).

source.quote:
Figure 7 shows that the Command A model is on the Pareto frontier between answering and refusing for both
safety modes.

findings.text: Relative safety (quality-aware) and absolute safety rankings diverge: Command A leads relative safety among large models but ranks third on absolute safety at 70.4% (higher is better).

source.quote:
Additionally, it attains an
absolute safety score of 70.4%, ranking third among large models, closely following Claude 3.5 Sonnet and

findings.text: When both responses are safe, relative safety judges prefer Command A's substantive answers over non-specific refusals such as Claude 3.5 Sonnet's.

source.quote:
Rather than simply refusing to answer, Command
A engages meaningfully with queries that relate to potentially unsafe topics. Many other models, such as
Claude 3.5 Sonnet, provide non-specific refusals.

findings.text: Command A is on the multilingual safety vs over-refusal Pareto frontier for Japanese, Chinese, German, Korean and Arabic.

source.quote:
Command A is on the Pareto frontier between safety and over-refusal in 5 languages (Japanese,
Chinese, German, Korean and Arabic), whilst remaining competitive in all other measured languages.

findings.text: Enterprise over-refusal sets were built by red-teaming Command R+ Refresh, so they are especially hard for Command A models.
